Ukraine says it urgently needs more U.S. Patriot interceptor missiles to defend
against incoming Russian attacks, but as NPR's Greg Myrie reports,
the paperwork to transfer them is stuck at the Pentagon.
A U.S. official confirmed to NPR that the authorization to send the Patriot missiles
to Ukraine is sitting on the desk of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon.
The official, who's not authorized to comment publicly on the issue,
spoke to NPR's Tom Bowman.
The story was first reported by The Washington Post.
The U.S. has stopped sending Patriots directly to Ukraine,
but some NATO countries have been willing to transfer small batches of 10 or so a month.
However, because these are U.S.-made weapons,
the Pentagon must sign off before they can be sent to Ukraine.
Russia can fire 20 or more missiles into Ukraine on a single night.
Greg Myrie, NPR News, Washington.
Early voting is underway in Texas. Democrats there hope they can pick up a Senate seat,
though it's been more than 30 years since a Democrat won a statewide race in Texas.
Houston Public Media's Andrew Schneider spoke with Republicans about their decision to support
Republican State Attorney General Ken Paxton over Democratic State Representative James Talarico.
Mark Petrichuk from Wood Forest, Texas, says he's supporting Paxton because he's not Talarico.
I'm a free market guy, and whoever is teaching these kids that socialism and communism is okay
are wrong, and so I'm actually voting against anybody that says they're a socialist or a communist.
Erika Johnson from the Woodlands says she's backing Paxton because of his record fighting
human trafficking as attorney general.
I do have a friend who was a victim of that,
and with his initiative, whenever he first became attorney general, that was really big on my heart.
Most polling shows the race between Paxton and Talarico is a statistical dead heat.
For NPR News, I'm Andrew Schneider in Houston.
General Motors says profits were up in its third quarter compared to last year,
but NPR's Willow Rubin reports electric vehicle sales were down.
Just over a year ago, a $7,500 federal tax credit that helped people buy and lease electric vehicles
went away. In an earnings call with analysts, GM executives said
that helps explain why its EV sales fell in the past year.
Data from Edmunds and Cox Automotive shows that's been true industry-wide.
But GM says it's continuing to make EVs.
Executives say GM is "right-sizing its capacity to align EV production with demand,"
and EV sales are growing abroad.
In Europe last year, over 30% of new cars sold were electric.
In China, more than half were. That's according to the International Energy Agency.
In the meantime, GM's gas-powered trucks helped make up for its losses.
Willow Rubin, NPR News.
Most of the U.S. stock market rose today following strong profit reports
from Equifax, Hasbro, and other companies. This is NPR.
Florida has conducted its 18th execution of the year. 77-year-old William Reeves died
by lethal injection. He's the eighth inmate over age 70, executed in Florida this year.
If another execution is carried out as planned in November,
Florida would tie its record. Set last year, Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis says
he wants to ensure justice is achieved for the families of victims
who've waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown says the state is suing prediction market
Cauchy seeking damages and keeping it from doing business in the state.
KUER's Hugo Ricard Bell reports.
Utah estimates Cauchy has made up to $61 million from alleged illegal wages placed by Utahns.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown wants the online company to pay it back.
Frankly, they are engineered to do one thing and one thing alone, and that is empty your wallet.
Prediction market apps like Cauchy blur the line between what is and isn't gambling.
However, Utah says it's clear-cut. Gambling of any kind is illegal in the state.
In a statement, Cauchy said they only answer to "federal law,"
and no single state should have a veto over it.
They say the Utah lawsuit won't hinder ongoing federal litigation.
For NPR News, I'm Hugo Ricard Bell in Salt Lake City.
Chicago's food delivery robots are facing legal challenges.
Two customers have filed lawsuits against Coco Robotics and Serv Robotics,
accusing them of collecting biometric data without consent.
The lawsuits claim the robots scanned faces and hands.
Both companies deny the allegations. This is NPR.
